slides.title: Module 6 review: physico-chemical and photometric methods
bullets: Material for biochemical testing is plasma, serum and other biological fluids; when enzymes are measured nothing that alters the fluid is added, and a highly active sample is diluted.
Centrifugation separates heavy parts by centrifugal force; an ultracentrifuge serves to determine molecular weight.
Electrophoresis separates charged particles in an electric field; it is used for serum protein analysis, and the amount of a fraction is proportional to staining intensity.
Chromatography separates mixtures: ion-exchange column, liquid, partition (paper) — substances are identified by the eluate or the Rf.
Colorimetry and photometry rest on the proportionality of colour intensity or light absorption to concentration; a photometer is more objective and sensitive than a colorimeter.
At an optical density of 1, 10% of the light passes; most methods are measured in a 1 cm cuvette.

slides.title: Module 6 review: basics of enzymes
bullets: Enzymes are biologically active proteins that speed up chemical reactions in the body.

Differences from inorganic catalysts: active under mild conditions (low temperature, normal pressure, a particular pH); speed the reaction up enormously; highly specific; their activity is regulated; reaction rate is directly proportional to the amount of enzyme.
Simple (protein only) and complex enzymes: a complex enzyme consists of an apoenzyme (protein part) and a cofactor (a metal ion or organic compound); together they form the active holoenzyme.
The active site has parts that bind the substrate (contact) and that catalyse the reaction (catalytic); some enzymes also have a regulatory (allosteric) site.

slides.title: Module 6 review: basics of enzymes
bullets: The dependence of enzyme activity on pH is bell-shaped: activity is maximal at the optimal pH; when activity is measured the optimal medium is set with buffer solutions; for most enzymes the optimal temperature is close to body temperature (37 °C).

As substrate concentration rises the reaction rate increases and reaches a maximum (Vmax); Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax; in the laboratory enzyme activity is measured at a saturating substrate concentration.

slides.title: Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
bullets: 1. Classification of carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose), oligosaccharides and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, fiber); complex carbohydrates – glycoproteins, glycosaminoglycans.

2. Biological significance: the main source of energy (glucose is the main substrate for the brain and erythrocytes), storage (glycogen), structural and receptor functions (glycoproteins, glycolipids).

3. Digestion: in the mouth salivary α-amylase starts it, in the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down starch, brush-border enzymes (maltase, isomaltase, sucrase, lactase) hydrolyze to monosaccharides.

4. Absorption: glucose and galactose – with Na⁺ via SGLT1 (secondary active transport), fructose – passively via GLUT5; from the enterocyte into the blood through basolateral transporters, then via the portal vein to the liver.

slides.title: Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
bullets: 5. Clinical-laboratory link: in lactase deficiency and other disaccharidase deficiencies – osmotic diarrhea; starch in stool (amylorrhea) – a sign of digestive insufficiency; blood glucose is measured by modern enzymatic methods (hexokinase, glucose oxidase).

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Glucose homeostasis: insulin (β cells) is the only glucose-lowering hormone: it enhances glucose entry into tissues, glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; counter-regulatory hormones – glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroid hormones.
2. Nervous system: sympathetic activity (adrenaline) enhances glycogenolysis and glucagon secretion; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) increase insulin secretion after a meal.
3. Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β cells, absolute insulin deficiency; markers: autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8), low C-peptide; tendency to ketoacidosis.
4. Type 2 DM – insulin resistance and relative insulin secretion deficiency; associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome; C-peptide initially normal/high.
5. Other types: gestational DM, monogenic (MODY), diseases of the exocrine pancreas, drug- or endocrinopathy-related.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 6. Diagnostic criteria are the same for both types: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT 2-hour value ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Diabetes criteria (ADA/WHO, venous plasma): fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 hours), 2-hour glucose at 75 g OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP-certified method standardized to DCCT), or random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms of hyperglycemia.
2. For a diagnosis without unequivocal hyperglycemia, two abnormal results are needed (two tests from one sample or on two different days).
3. Prediabetes (ADA): fasting 5.6–6.9 mmol/L (impaired fasting glucose), OGTT 2-hour 7.8–11.0 (impaired glucose tolerance), HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

4. Conditions in which HbA1c is unreliable: sickle cell and other hemoglobinopathies (method-dependent), second–third trimester of pregnancy, hemodialysis, recent blood loss/transfusion, erythropoietin therapy, G6PD deficiency, HIV – in these only plasma glucose is used.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 5. Preanalytics: because of glycolysis, glucose at room temperature falls by ~5–7% per hour – centrifuge the sample immediately or use a tube with a glycolysis inhibitor; a glucometer result is not for diagnosis.

6. Determining type and complications: autoantibodies, C-peptide; ketones; urine albumin/creatinine ratio, eGFR, lipids; in pregnancy at 24–28 weeks a 75 g OGTT (92/180/153 mg/dL ≈ 5.1/10.0/8.5 mmol/L).
